questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl at the GP has short stature, a low posterior hairline and widely spaced nipples. Her mother recalls a doctor once heard a soft heart murmur that was never followed up. You are examining her cardiovascular system with a chaperone present. Which bedside step best screens her for coarctation of the aorta?
options: Measure blood pressure lying and then standing after three minutes
Feel right radial and femoral pulses together for delay, and compare arm and leg BP
Listen at the apex with the bell, with her rolled into the left lateral position
Palpate the carotid pulse for a slow-rising, low-volume character
questions.why: Coarctation narrows the aorta, usually just past the left subclavian artery. This delays and weakens the femoral pulse compared with the right radial and makes leg BP lower than arm BP. Coarctation is a key cardiac lesion in Turner syndrome, so check radio-femoral delay and four-limb BP.
notes: A postural BP drop screens for volume depletion or autonomic dysfunction, not for an obstruction between the arm and leg circulations.
The left lateral position with the bell brings out mitral stenosis and low-pitched sounds, not the delay in leg perfusion that coarctation causes.
A slow-rising carotid pulse suggests significant aortic stenosis. It does not detect coarctation, which spares the carotid and right arm pulses.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl has 45,X Turner syndrome. FSH is 58 IU/L, LH 24 IU/L and oestradiol is below 40 pmol/L. She has no breast development, and her bone age is 11 years with open growth plates. She is to start growth hormone. Her mother asks how puberty will be brought on. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Wait until she is 15 years old in case puberty starts on its own before treating
Start the combined oral contraceptive pill now to bring on breasts and periods
Endocrinology-led low-dose transdermal oestradiol, increased gradually over 2 to 3 years
Start full adult-dose oestradiol now, with a cyclical progestogen from the start
questions.why: Puberty induction in Turner syndrome is led by paediatric endocrinology. It starts at about 11 to 12 years with low-dose (usually transdermal) oestradiol, increased slowly over 2 to 3 years, with a progestogen added later. This keeps growth potential and gives good breast, uterine and bone development.
notes: Her raised gonadotrophins show ovarian failure, so puberty is very unlikely to start on its own. Waiting delays bone and breast development and adds to her distress.
The pill's ethinylestradiol dose is too high to begin with. It closes the growth plates early and gives poorer breast and uterine development than gradual oestradiol.
A full dose from the start fuses the growth plates early and causes poor breast shape. A progestogen is only added after about 2 years of oestrogen, or once breakthrough bleeding occurs.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl with 45,X Turner syndrome has no breast development. Her bloods show FSH 58 IU/L and LH 24 IU/L, both far above the prepubertal range, with oestradiol below 40 pmol/L. Her free T4 is normal. Which mechanism best explains her raised gonadotrophins?
options: Accelerated loss of ovarian follicles removes oestradiol and inhibin negative feedback
A pituitary gonadotroph adenoma secretes FSH and LH autonomously
Her raised TSH cross-reacts with FSH receptors and drives gonadotrophin release
Early activation of hypothalamic GnRH pulses, with normal ovarian follicle reserve
questions.why: In 45,X, ovarian follicles die off quickly and the ovaries become streak gonads. Without follicles there is little oestradiol or inhibin B to suppress the hypothalamus and pituitary, so FSH and LH rise. This is hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.
notes: Gonadotroph adenomas are rare in children, usually make little active hormone and would cause headaches or visual change. Her picture is fully explained by ovarian failure.
TSH cross-reacting with the FSH receptor (Van Wyk-Grumbach syndrome) needs severe hypothyroidism and causes early puberty. Her TSH is only mildly raised and her free T4 is normal.
If her ovaries had normal follicles, the GnRH drive would raise oestradiol and start breast development. Her oestradiol is low and she has no breast development.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl with Turner syndrome has a renal ultrasound. It shows the lower poles of both kidneys joined across the midline, in front of the aorta, by an isthmus of renal tissue, with both halves lying low. During embryonic ascent of the kidneys, which structure usually stops the isthmus from rising?
questions.why: In a horseshoe kidney, the fused lower poles form an isthmus in front of the aorta. As the kidneys ascend from the pelvis, the isthmus catches under the inferior mesenteric artery, so the kidneys lie low. This is why both halves of her horseshoe kidney sit low and are malrotated.
notes: The coeliac trunk arises at about T12, well above where the kidneys finish their ascent, so it does not trap the isthmus.
The SMA arises at about L1, above the level where a horseshoe kidney gets stuck. The SMA is better known for compressing the left renal vein (nutcracker syndrome).
The left renal vein drains the kidney into the IVC. It does not lie in the path of the ascending isthmus, so it does not stop it rising.
